title: 1 Chronicles 10:1–7
context: The Chronicler begins his narrative history with Saul’s last battle. The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa and kill Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. Wounded and distressed by the archers, Saul asks his armor bearer to kill him; when the armor bearer refuses in fear, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer does the same. Israel’s men in the valley abandon their cities to the Philistines. The parallel is 1 Samuel 31:1–7, with some differences in wording; for example, 1 Chronicles 10:6 says that all Saul’s house died together, where 1 Samuel 31:6 names his armor bearer and his men. The different account given by an Amalekite in 2 Samuel 1:6–10 is not part of this chapter and is not harmonized here.

verses.text: Now the Philistines fought against Israel; and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, and Israel’s men fall. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler begins his narrative with a defeat, setting Saul’s end as the backdrop for David’s rise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the battle as the beginning of God’s transfer of the kingdom, which the Chronicler explains in 10:13–14. Shared ground: the verse closely follows 1 Samuel 31:1, and both traditions read it soberly as national disaster.

verses.text: The Philistines followed hard after Saul and after his sons; and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines pursue Saul and his sons and kill Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. Arminian readers note the grief of Jonathan’s death in particular, given his friendship with David and his faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the death of Saul’s sons as part of the end of his dynasty. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Samuel 31:2, with the Chronicler’s wording “followed hard after” in place of “overtook” in Samuel.

verses.text: The battle went hard against Saul, and the archers overtook him; and he was distressed by reason of the archers.
verses.arminianNotes: The battle goes hard against Saul, and the archers wound him. Arminian readers note the human detail of the king’s distress, which the narrative reports without mockery or harshness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king who once stood head and shoulders above the people now brought low. Shared ground: the verse parallels 1 Samuel 31:3, and both traditions read it as a sober account of Saul’s final hour.

verses.text: Then Saul said to his armor bearer, “Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and abuse me.” But his armor bearer would not, for he was terrified. Therefore Saul took his sword and fell on it.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks his armor bearer to kill him, and when he refuses, Saul falls on his sword. Arminian readers handle the scene pastorally, as the 1 Samuel 31:4 notes do, noting Saul’s fear of abuse by his enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the account soberly and do not speculate about Saul’s final destiny. Both traditions note that 2 Samuel 1:6–10 records a different account from the Amalekite, which is noted rather than harmonized here.

verses.text: When his armor bearer saw that Saul was dead, he likewise fell on his sword and died.
verses.arminianNotes: The armor bearer, seeing Saul dead, also falls on his sword and dies. Arminian readers note the loyalty of a servant who would not outlive his master, reported without comment by the Chronicler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the armor bearer’s death as completing the tragic scene. Shared ground: the verse closely follows 1 Samuel 31:5, and both traditions read it with restraint, avoiding judgment beyond what the text says.

verses.text: So Saul died with his three sons; and all his house died together.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul dies with his three sons, and all his house dies together. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler summarizes the end of Saul’s house more broadly than 1 Samuel 31:6, which names his armor bearer and his men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase as the Chronicler’s way of marking the end of Saul’s dynasty as a ruling house. Both traditions note that a son of Saul later reigned briefly (2 Samuel 2:8–10), and they read the summary without forcing a resolution.

verses.text: When all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that they fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities, and fled; and the Philistines came and lived in them.
verses.arminianNotes: When the men of Israel in the valley see the defeat, they abandon their cities to the Philistines. Arminian readers note the wider cost of Saul’s defeat for ordinary Israelites, who lose their homes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss of cities as showing how far Israel had fallen at the end of Saul’s reign. Shared ground: the verse parallels 1 Samuel 31:7, which also mentions those beyond the Jordan; the Chronicler’s version is shorter.
